r16|A|1.head: Icebreakers Impress
r16|A|1.html:
It was a poor start in Group A for the defending champions, the Hungarian Shamans, starting behind as Ecuador started on the committee, Tahiti blitzing away from the pin, with Estonia in the middle.

The Estonian Icebreakers, so impressive in the 1/32 Finals, overhauled the Tahitian Black Pearls upwind, and the Shamans ground their way back into the game to round the top mark in second.

Downwind the fleet put the throttle down, showing impressive crewwork in the challenging conditions as white water rushed over the decks, hitting in excess of 17 knots at times. The grinders were pushed to the limit as the trimmers worked the spinnakers. This was sailing on the very edge of control.

While the grinders provided the brawn, the tacticians’ brains were similarly worked, connecting the windshifts as the rain clouds passed overhead. Every element of sailing skill was being tested.

The Icebreakers extended again, looking right at home in the conditions, while the Black Pearls closed on the Shamans upwind, rounding just 10 seconds behind at the final windward mark.

Estonia went on to win by a huge margin, while Hungary just held off Tahiti’s attack, and Ecuador have work to do to make an impact in this ultra-competitive group.

day.t: Wet and Wild Opener to the Copa do Mundo da Vela 1/16 Finals
day.intro:
It was a very different Rio that greeted the arriving nations in the Copa do Mundo da Vela with the sunshine replaced by rain, and murky clouds hiding the the peak of Sugarloaf Mountain and Christ the Redeemer on Mount Corcovado.

The wind though was in, with 15 to 17 knots on Guanabara Bay, from the south-southwest.

r16|B|1.head: Ice Cool Chile Conquer the Monsoon
r16|B|1.html:
With the wind hitting 20 knots for Group B, Chile speared across the start line while Portugal forced Malaysia to tack off early as South Africa lagged at the back, looking ragged in the gusts.

The wind was up and down like a yo-yo, mainsails flogging in the gusts, down to just 10 knots in the lulls, making watching the wind an imperative.

There were problems about the South African Ubuntu yacht as the trim tab came off the keel, with the shore team quickly coming out to help, but putting them out of the race.

The Chilean team were excelling, closely followed by the Portuguese Navigators at the windward mark, but a monumental broach during their first gybe saw them briefly lose second to the Malaysian Monsoon team. The error clearly fired up the Navigators, hitting the afterburners to overhaul the Monsoon team in a wall of spray.

The charging Navigators continued their resurgence on the final upwind leg, closing right on the Chilean Finis Terrae team, powering past them to take the lead.

The two then match raced as the wind dropped up the course but, with the attention on each other, the Malaysian Monsoon team found great breeze on the right to jump into the lead.

Coming into the final windward mark it was anyone’s game in the shifts and gusts, with Malaysia tacking just beneath Portugal on the starboard layline with Chile just behind.

The teams were on tenterhooks hoisting their spinnakers, with Malaysia ahead as Chile shot past Portugal who had a slow hoist. Chile and Portugal gybed early as Malaysia fell out of the breeze on the right.

The big breeze on the left saw Chile power to the win, with Portugal once again deploying their submarine mode as water rushed over the deck to take second ahead of the unlucky Malaysia team.

day.intro:
It was a very different Rio that greeted the arriving nations in the Copa do Mundo da Vela with the sunshine replaced by rain, and murky clouds hiding the the peak of Sugarloaf Mountain and Christ the Redeemer on Mount Corcovado.

The wind though was in, with 15 to 17 knots on Guanabara Bay, from the south-southwest.

It was a long and exciting Friday with six incredible races at the Copa do Mundo da Vela, the Football World Cup in Sailing, followed by a visit to the Maracanã Stadium, the venue of the 2014 FIFA World Cup Final, to watch Fluminense play Cruzeiro.

With the breeze already in from the southerly sea breeze direction at 10 to 12 knots, another superb day was on the cards.

r16|C|2.head: Assured Ambers go Back-to-Back
r16|C|2.html:
After a short delay, Group C started their second race with the wind setting at its familiar southerly direction and building to 10 knots.

Japan aimed for a port-tack flyer, but had to duck under the fleet, as Lithuania closed in on the pin end. The fleet tacked to port early in a left hand shift, forcing Thailand into the Ambers’ disturbed air, which they endured for a while before tacking away.

The well-drilled Lithuanian team rounded the top mark first, with Thailand coming in on the port layline to squeeze in the gap between Japan and Myanmar.

Positions remained the same at the leeward gate, with the course rotated 15 degrees to the left. The gradually building breeze saw all the athletes hiking hard in the gusts to gain every ounce of speed from their yachts. Japan and Thailand were trading second place regularly on the second upwind leg after choosing different buoys at the leeward gate, with Thailand making big gains approaching the final windward mark.

The final downwind leg saw Lithuania consolidate their lead in the group as Thailand held off Japan's high mode charge to take second, with Myanmar this time at the back.

day.intro:
What a difference a day makes! Guanabara Bay presented a very different race course to that of Thursday. Gone were the rain and squally winds, replaced with clouds, combined with a patchy and shifty wind from the south-east, ready to test tacticians’ tenacity.

An ambitious six races were on the schedule to get things back on track after the storm.

r16|D|1.head: Uruguay’s Olympians Inspire
r16|D|1.html:
The breeze swung back round to the south-east for Group D’s opener with Peru winning the pin, forcing Uruguay to tack off early, and the Czech Republic taking the early lead, making the best of the shifting winds.

Uruguay’s Olympic 49er pairing of Hernán Umpierre and Fernando Diz have transitioned their teamwork beautifully to the larger crew on the SSL47 yachts, and the athletes worked as one to find the best approach to the windward mark and execute a perfect hoist, taking the lead ahead of the Czech Lakers, while Ukraine held off Peru downwind for third at the leeward gate.

The second upwind leg saw the teams unanimously favouring the right, with Ukraine closing in on and then passing the Czech Republic team who had a twist in their spinnaker on the hoist, while it was disaster for Peru, languishing after the kite went into the water ahead of the hoist, stalling the boat.

Uruguay cruised to the win, but the battle to the finish between the Czechs and Ukraine was nail-biting. Rodion Luka had taken his team left downwind, and the yachts converged with an overlap, leading to the Czech Republic gybing when calling the layline to take second, just 6 seconds ahead of Ukraine, as Peru limped to the line after the spinnaker troubles.

r16|D|2.head: Rodion Luka’s downwind masterclass
r16|D|2.html:
Peru got it all wrong at the pin end in Group D’s second race, lining up early and then sliding sideways, forcing them to tack behind the Czech Republic while Uruguay and Ukraine lined up in the middle. Uruguay’s La Celeste team then had to tack as Ukraine’s United team climbed up to their line.

At the top mark it was the Czechs who rounded ahead of Ukraine with Uruguay trailing the pair ahead of Peru. At the leeward gate there was a split choice of buoys, leading to a tense anticipation as Ukraine tacked in from the right, but Ondra Teply’s Czech Lakers held firm, crossing ahead.

At the final windward mark the lead was 15 seconds, but Rodion Luka’s Ukraine team went deep after the spinnaker hoist, effectively blocking the Czechs from gybing and setting up a grandstand finish while Uruguay charged behind, but had nearly 100 metres to make up on the top two.

The frontrunners gybed simultaneously, with Ukraine snatching the lead from the Czechs, as Uruguay came right back into the game.

The final gybe into the finish saw Ukraine charge again, taking the win by 6 seconds from the Czechs with Uruguay a further 15 seconds back with Peru needing to improve their teamwork to compete in this strong group.

r16|A|2.head: Drama at every turn!
r16|A|2.html:
A picture-perfect start in Group A’s second race saw the teams cross the line simultaneously as Ecuador won the committee boat end and Tahiti powered off the pin.

Two minutes after the start there was disaster for the defending SSL Gold Cup champions, the Hungarian Shamans, as their bowman went overboard, dropping them 150 metres behind the fleet as they recovered their crewmate from the water.

As commentator Yann Dorset said on the YouTube livestream, it was a ‘game of snakes and ladders’ as Tahiti and Ecuador battled at the front with Estonia employed a high mode to climb and, remarkably, Hungary squeezed in on the port layline to round the top mark in second with just 19 seconds separating first from last.

Snakes and ladders became cat and mouse downwind as the crews jostled, gybed and strategised and the leaderboard continually shuffled. The Tahiti Black Pearls left their spinnaker drop to the last second to round ahead of Hungary and Estonia while Ecuador went for the left hand buoy, which proved to be a costly mistake.

World Champions Hungary gradually climbed towards Tahiti, eventually forcing them to tack away, as Mati Sepp and his Estonian Icebreakers quietly gained on the left.

The Icebreakers charged into the gap on port, tacking right on Tahiti’s bow, but the umpires raised the red flag and intriguingly both boats completed a penalty in unison.

All this drama played right into Zsombor Berecz’s hands as the Shamans powered away to the win, with Tahiti regaining second from the Icebreakers.

This was breathless Copa do Mundo da Vela racing at its best.

r16|B|2.head: Cool Monsoon team close out a great day
r16|B|2.html:
South Africa and Portugal made the best starts to Group B’s second race, and after another closely-fought upwind leg Portugal rounded just ahead of Malaysia after coming in from the left as the Monsoon team asked for a Navigators penalty, but the umpires green flagged it.

Downwind positions remained steady, with everyone favouring the right, and the fleet was tightly packed at the leeward gate.

There was no way of separating Malaysia and Portugal upwind with the Monsoon just pipping the Navigators as they both came into the final windward mark on the port layline.

Team Malaysia’s teamwork was exceptional, hoisting the spinnaker with such speed that they pulled out two boat lengths on Portugal, as both South Africa and Chile closed in on the leaders.

The Monsoon team were as cool as a cucumber downwind, protecting their lead to take the win, while the Navigators went into defensive mode to just hold off the South African Ubuntu team’s charge.
